title: Corporate social responsibility

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the 1980s, Norwegian Prime Minister Gro Harlem Brundtland gave the following definition of corporate social responsibility (CSR): 'Meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.' Nowadays, governments, activists and the media are quick to hold companies to account for the social consequences of their actions. As a result, corporate social responsibility has become a priority for business leaders around the world. When a well-run business applies its vast resources and expertise to social problems that it understands and in which it has a stake, it can have a greater impact than any other organization. Although many companies have already done much to improve the social and environmental impact of their activities, these efforts are not always as productive as they could be.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: To advance CSR we need first to acknowledge the interrelationship between a corporation and society. Successful corporations need a healthy society. Education, health care and equal opportunities are essential to a productive workforce. Safe products and working conditions not only attract customers but also lower internal costs as there are fewer accidents, while good government and strong regulatory standards protect both consumers and competing companies from exploitation. Ultimately, a healthy society creates demand for business as more human needs are met and aspirations grow. At the same time, a healthy society needs successful companies to create the jobs, wealth and innovation that improve social conditions over time.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A company's impact on society also changes over time, as social standards evolve and science progresses. Asbestos, now understood to be a serious health risk, was thought to be safe in the early 1900s, given the scientific knowledge then available. Evidence of its risks gradually mounted for more than 50 years before any company was held liable for the harm it can cause. Many firms that failed to anticipate the consequences of this evolving body of research have been bankrupted by the results. No longer can companies be content to monitor only the obvious social impacts of today. Without a careful process to identify evolving social effects, firms may risk their very survival.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: However, no business can solve all of society's problems or bear the cost of doing so. Instead, each company must choose issues that intersect with its particular business. Other social agendas are best left to companies in other industries or government institutions that are better positioned to address them. The essential test that should guide CSR is not whether a cause is worthy but whether it presents an opportunity to create shared value - that is, a meaningful benefit for society that is also valuable for the business. Each company should try to identify the social problems that it is best equipped to help resolve. Addressing social issues in this way will lead to self-sustaining solutions that are not dependent on government subsidies.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The best corporate citizenship initiatives involve far more than simply donating money; they specify clear goals and measure their effectiveness over time. A good example is the manufacturing company GE's program to adopt public high schools in poorer areas near several of its major US facilities. The company contributes between $250,000 and $1 million over a five-year period to each school. GE's managers and employees take an active role by working with school administrators to assess needs and tutor students. GE conducted a study of ten schools in the program between 1989 and 1999 and nearly all showed significant improvement in their academic standards. Programs such as this one create goodwill and improve relations with local governments. Their effect is inherently limited, however. No matter how beneficial the program is, it remains incidental to the company's manufacturing business, and the direct effect on GE's recruiting and retention is modest.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Software company Microsoft's partnership with the American Association of Community Colleges is a good example of a mutually beneficial opportunity. The shortage of information technology workers is a significant constraint on Microsoft's growth; currently there are 450,000 unfilled IT positions in the US alone. Community colleges with an enrollment of 11.6 million students, representing 45% of all US undergraduates, could provide a solution. Microsoft recognizes, however, that these colleges face special challenges: IT curricula are not standardized, technology used in classrooms is often outdated, and there are no professional development programs to keep teachers up to date. Microsoft's $50 million, five-year initiative was aimed at all three problems. In addition to contributing money and products, Microsoft sent employee volunteers to colleges to assess needs and contribute to curriculum development. Microsoft's program benefited many communities while also having a clear impact on company profits.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: A final example is the company Whole Foods Market. Its aim is to sell organic, healthy food to customers who are passionate about food and the environment. The company sources all of its products from local farmers and screens out up to 100 common ingredients that it considers to be unhealthy or environmentally damaging. Furthermore, Whole Foods' stores are constructed using a majority of recycled materials and the company recently bought renewable wind energy credits equal to 100% of its electricity use. Any spoiled produce is trucked to regional centers for composting and all of their vehicles are being converted to biofuels. In this initiative, even the cleaning products used in their stores are environmentally friendly. In short, the entire company's operations reinforce its ideals, helping to distinguish Whole Foods from its competitors.
